content.title: Looking forward to your post-rebuttal feedback
content.comment:
Dear ACs and reviewers:

Thanks again for all of your constructive suggestions, which have helped us improve the quality and clarity of the paper!

The author-reviewer discussion period will end soon in one day. We appreciate it if you take the time to read our rebuttal and give us some feedback. Please don’t hesitate to let us know if there are any additional clarifications or experiments that we can offer, as we would love to convince you of the merits of the paper. We appreciate your suggestions.

Thanks for your time and efforts.

Best,\
Authors

Dear Reviewer 7Fv1,

Thanks again for your insightful suggestions and comments. As the deadline for discussion will end soon in one day, we are happy to provide any additional clarifications that you may need. In our rebuttal, we have carefully studied your comments and made detailed responses. Particularly, we have added new experiment results to answer Q1 and Q4.

Please do not hesitate to contact us if there are other clarifications or experiments we can offer. 

Thank you for your time!

Best,\
Authors

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers unsupervised continual learning (UCL) for SimSiam architecture using memory/rememory procedure. The proposed method is quite simple but it is shown to achieve good empirical performance. It is not a major breakthrough, but the positive experimental results have some value.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Proposed method is simple and easy to implement. 
- Experimental results are thorough and provide detailed analyses on ablation study, hyperparameter selection, and visualization. 
- The performance gain against baseline exists. 

Weakness
- The proposed method is similar to the method in [Schwarz et al., Progress & Compress: A scalable framework for continual learning, ICML 2018] and can be thought of as yet another regularization based method combined with the replay memory. 
- The method needs to maintain the two models together with the replay memory. For a fair comparison, the memory requirements among baselines should be also done. If the method without memory can use much larger capacity of a model, then the shown performance gap could be closed. Please provide this comparison in the rebuttal.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall method and presentation is clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: As mentioned in the above comment, the proposed method is not a major breakthrough, but it is showing some performance gain compared to other UCL methods. But, I think a critical component is the memory requirement for different method since the proposed method needs to maintain two equivalent models. This requirement could let other methods to use more replay memory or larger model architecture when fair memory comparison needs to be done. I would like to make my final judgment based on this result and also will consult other reviewers as well.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a new idea for Unsupervised Continual Learning (UCL) without replay buffer, named RM-SimSiam. RM-SimSiam stores old knowledge in a historical module and then transfer the knowledge from historical module to the current model. An additional contrastive loss is further proposed to align the feature representations between the historical and the current models. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is well-written and quite easy to follow.
- The idea of rehearsal-free is important, and saving past knowledge in a parametrized module instead of buffer is intuitive.
- The whole framework is simple and concise.

Weaknesses:
- One of the main weaknesses is actually the knowledge transfer process defined in (5-6). The target model is simply defined as the linear combination of the current and the historical model, which seems a bit counter intuitive for me. Since neural networks are non-linear models, superposition of two networks cannot be treated as a *combination* of two networks. Therefore, I think more intuition and theoretical insights should be given to better explain *why* the knowledge transfer actually works.
- Also, the intuition of ESC loss is somewhat vague. It seems that it is doing a modified version of *distillation* from the historical model to the current model. Then, why it is superior than the distillation-based losses?
- For the ablation study, I wonder why every model (besides the base one) requires Mixup, which is not a proposed component of the work. 
- The insight from the visualization result is a bit hard to get.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and quality of the paper is good.
The novelty of the paper is a bit incremental.
The reproducibility of the paper is a bit questionable. Since contrastive-based models are not easy to learn, and the proposed method is ultimately heuristic, I think the results requires double check after releasing the codebase.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an important and interesting problem, unsupervised continual learning. Although the results are good, the intuition and theoretical justification behind the method is not that strong.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to duplicate the network to have two exponential moving average processes to alleviate the effect of forgetting in unsupervised continual learning. The results report a small gain of performance on continual CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet benchmarks. The model design seems complicated and not fully justified, meanwhile an important comparison to BYOL is missing. While the main motivation is to reduce the memory consumption of an extra data buffer, the best performer still uses the data buffer, and even worse the overhead introduced by the model duplicate can actually be much more expensive than storing a buffer size of 256 images.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of the paper is that it is studying an interesting topic of unsupervised continual learning, and the memory mechanism is an important area to investigate under this topic.

The main weakness of the paper is the lack of a simpler principle in its model design. First of all, for studying the momentum averaging technique, the paper should at least cite and compare BYOL (Grill et al. 2020). There are some minor differences that in BYOL it uses a momentum averaging term in each view, whereas here the two views are duplicated and become four views, but BYOL is just a simpler design. Avoiding the discussion of BYOL in the paper seems questionable.

Secondly, the re-memory mechanism seems very complicated without reason. Since the two branches are averages of each other, there is no reason calling one to be “new” and the other to be “history”. I hypothesize that the re-memory mechanism is functionally similar to having a very large momentum term that is close to 1.0 (in fact, BYOL uses a momentum of 0.99 - 0.999). I will actually show that the re-memory mechanism is equivalent to momentum = 1.0 at steady state. And this should give us an idea what might happen in the transient state too.

Suppose there is no gradient update and the two networks are just performing moving averages of each other (i.e. re-memory). For notational convenience, let the parameter of one network be $x$ and the other be $y$. $t$ denotes the timestep. Let $m$ be the momentum decay rate. Without loss of generality, we can let $y$ update first and rewrite $x_t$ as a function of $x_{t-1}$:
\begin{align}
y_t &= m y_{t-1} + (1-m) x_{t-1} \\\\
x_t &= m x_{t-1} + (1-m) y_{t}
\end{align}

Then we rewrite $x_t$ in terms of $x_{t-1}$:
\begin{align}
x_t &= m x_{t-1} + (1-m) y_{t} \\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m) \left[m y_{t-1} + (1-m) x_{t-1} \right] \\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m)^2 x_{t-1} + m(1-m) y_{t-1} \\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m)^2 x_{t-1} + m(1-m) \left[m y_{t-2} + (1-m) x_{t-2} \right]\\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m)^2 x_{t-1} + m(1-m)^2 x_{t-2} + m^2(1-m)^2 y_{t-2} \\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (1-m)^2 m^r x_{t-1-r}.
\end{align}

Now we show that suppose $x_t = x_{t-1}$, then we can get the equivalent relation.
\begin{align}
x_t &= x_{t-1}\\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m) x_{t-1}\\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m) x_{t}\\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m)^2 x_{t-1} + m (1-m) x_{t-1} \\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + (1-m)^2 x_{t-1} + m (1-m)^2 x_{t-2} + m^2 ( 1-m) x_{t-2} \\\\
&= m x_{t-1} + \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (1-m)^2 m^r x_{t-1-r}.
\end{align}

Therefore, at steady state, the re-memory mechanism converges to an identity operator $x_t = x_{t-1}$. This also suggests that in the transient state, it functions as if it has a very large momentum term that is close to 1 (e.g. 0.999), since in the transient state we can approximate it by truncating some tail terms.

Third, it is unclear whether the gain might come from the fact that the losses are added together instead of averaged. So the basic SimSiam will have only two terms whereas the proposed model has six terms, which makes the loss values three times as large, and also makes the gradient three times as large.

Last but not least, while the main motivation, as written in the introduction, is to reduce the memory consumption of an extra data buffer, the best performer still uses the data buffer, and even worse the overhead introduced by the model duplicate can actually be much more expensive than storing a buffer size of 256 images. The model duplication design seems to defeat the purpose of getting rid of a data buffer, but I acknowledge the additional benefit of memory momentum on top of a data buffer.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is less clear in the notation of separate branches, f, g, h, q, and the loss indices i, j. I often get lost reading the notations and loss terms, possibly due to the added complexity of the model without a simpler principle underneath.

Although the novelty appears to be the re-memory mechanism, as I explained above, it might functionally be equivalent to a large momentum term, and therefore further investigation is necessary for claiming it being a new and useful mechanism.

In terms of reproducibility, the paper promised to release their implementation soon.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summary, I am not fully convinced by the model design. It might be functionally equivalent to a much simpler momentum model. Comparison to BYOL is more than necessary in the future version. Investigation in terms of adding vs. averaging the losses should be carefully done. And the re-memory design defeats the purpose of getting rid of a data buffer. Based on these concerns, I do not recommend the acceptance of this current version of the paper.

----
I acknowledge that I read the rebuttal and thank the authors for the updated results. I decide to raise my score from 3 to 5. But the additional experiment still does not hide the drawback that storing an extra model is still more expensive than 256 images, and the added benefit is small compared to LUMP or SI.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper talks about unsupervised continual learning in scenarios where storage is limited. They proposed a rememory-based method RM-SimSiam by storing and remembering the old knowledge with a data-free historical module instead of replay buffer. To further improve the rememory ability of our RM-SimSiam, they devised an enhanced SimSiam-based contrastive loss by aligning the representations outputted
by the historical and new models. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets are reported and discussed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
Overall the paper is well written and clearly organized. The technical details are easy to follow.
RM-SimSiam outperforms the other baseline models with a higher accuracy and a lower forgetting rate.

Cons:
Three hyperparameters m, $\alpha$, $\lambda$ are used to consolidate and remember the learned knowledge, and they are working in  different mechanics. I would like to see how these three hyperparameters affect the learning features, like why their impacts are complimentary to each other? If we fix m and increase $\alpha$ or we fix $\alpha$ and increase m, can we add a tsne-plot to visualize the features?

Another point is the rememory mechianism for UCL seems like the exponential moving average trick in MOCO, and this trick is proved to be not necessary in self-supervised learning in SimSiam. Could you please elaborate on this part a little more?


Minor mistakes:
Efficient Lifelong Learning with A-GEM in ICLR 2019
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper proposed the method mainly based on the SimSiam paper but they made a few modifications. Though effective, the motivations of such modifications are not fully stated. It seems like some loaded tricks and they finetuned the hyperparameters to find a satisfying result. I just wish more discussions on why they chose to make such modifications and maybe some experimental comparison on toy data to illustrate the motivations concretely.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I find the paper very easy to read and presenting some interesting ideas and even some exciting improvements in performance. I want to see more detailed discussion on the motivations and how these motivations lead to the modifications.

content.title: Rememory-Based SimSiam for Unsupervised Continual Learning
content.TL;DR: We propose a novel rememory-based SimSiam method for unsupervised continual learning.
content.abstract: Unsupervised continual learning (UCL) has started to draw attention from the continual learning community, motivated by the practical need of representation learning with unlabeled data on sequential tasks. However, most of recent UCL methods focus on mitigating the catastrophic forgetting problem with a replay buffer to store previous data (i.e., rehearsal-based strategy), which needs much extra storage and thus limits their practical applications. To overcome this drawback, based on contrastive learning via SimSiam, we propose a novel rememory-based SimSiam (RM-SimSiam) method to reduce the dependency on replay buffer under the UCL setting. The core idea of our RM-SimSiam is to store and remember the old knowledge with a data-free historical module instead of replay buffer. Specifically, this historical module is designed to store the historical average model of all previous models (i.e., the memory process) and then transfer the knowledge of the historical average model to the new model (i.e., the rememory process). To further improve the rememory ability of our RM-SimSiam, we devise an enhanced SimSiam-based contrastive loss by aligning the representations outputted by the historical and new models. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our RM-SimSiam under the UCL setting.
